"On the question of whether Smith Construction," she read, naming the contractor, "was negligent in the upgrading of 418 Hartwell Street," she continued, "we the jury find the defendant . . ." The lawyer put his hand on Celia's arm, and she was against the chair, trying not to tremble as he whispered in her ear. " . . . not guilty."

Celia Medina tried to behave. She didn't get angry. So she sat very still while the judge and the jurors thanked each other and shook hands and left the courtroom. She didn't touch her food when they walked out to street level and were met by a row of TV vans and reporters, the lawyers who represented the tenants shouting into cell phones. Mr. Boateng walked slowly beside her, dropping money onto the sidewalk. Celia, the landlord's lawyer said into his black phone, had provided ineffective notice of the problem.

Now it was night and she was a block from home, listening to the ticking of the crosswalk sign as cars sped by like an ocean swell. She thought about setting a fire to Hartwell Properties, the office that leased apartments for $600 a month with holes and sparky wiring and dime-sized bottles of dish soap. She didn't want a lawyer anymore. She wanted to burn the place down. To see them feel what she felt when she saw her landlord's name on the TV vans.

She touched her skin around her right eye. It burned.

As Celia Medina walked into the house, Uncle Mamdie was standing in the parlor. He was a short, straight-backed man in jodhpurs and a helmet-shaped hat. His hands, which had held a cigar and then the reins of racehorses for sixty years, were cracked and callused. When Celia was seven, and Mamdie lived in Humanville, he'd taken her on walks around the beet-colored streets to the fields and swamps beyond the suburbs. That was before he married Helen Kane and then Jackie Thompson; before he moved out west and then moved back.

"Chi-chi," Mamdie said when he saw Celia on the street. So she couldn't help smiling at him.

Thanks for kindly notice of your intention, Auntie Helen frayed from the frame above him. Celia had wanted to hang her own picture there, something of her own house, but Mamdie never got around to it

The defendant was guilty. The jury awarded $11.4 million for the lawsuit, over a million dollars for each person or family permanently dispossessed by the fire.

They had proved the property was dangerous; they proved the owner had let people live there even with those conditions; they even proved how much some tenants had lost. But Celia never asked what it meant. Winning an $11 million judgment in New York City is like winning a Congressional medal of honor: Everyone knows what it should mean, no one knows what it will. More fights would follow, this time with tenant rights lawyers and moneymen.

Kevin Zuckerman's job was to get money. He was a middle-aged Jewish man from the Bronx who walked with one leg shorter than the other. He was also a linebacker 6'4" and 250 pounds. The tenants whooped and stomped their feet, and Mr. Boateng clapped Celia on the back. The jury foreperson read from another sheet of paper. "On the question of electrical safety," she read, "the jury finds that Hartwell Properties was negligent and that this negligence was the proximate cause of the 2001 fire which occurred at 418 Hartwell Street." The tenants whooped and stomped.
(Hartwell Properties was eventually sold to doctors, lawyers, and hedge-fund managers, but the jury's ruling still allows the tenants to sue.)

Celia didn't stop calling lawyers until she found Luis Gashano, a partner at Hughes Mathews Cohen, personal injury and wrongful death big rigs, who listened to her story and said they'd look into it, on contingency. She gave him all her papers and all her notes, and he researched it. When he showed up in her small rent-stabilized apartment on the Lower East Side and said Hartwell had committed criminal fraud in their attempt to kill the jury's award, she listened.

They went to court again. They talked to more police and more fire officials. They went to the bank and got Celia's mortgage payoff. They filed complaints with the state's Department of Financial Institutions. Eight months later they had enough: that Hartwell had known there were problems with their own electrical work before Celia moved in, that they'd given her a dangerous apartment, on purpose, to lure her into buying the place, that they'd used forged documents to close the deal, and that they'd committed arson to hide their crimes.

Three years after that, on the day they reached the settlement with Hartwell, they finally threw the party. Celia danced with her sons, with Luis Gashano and his wife, with her building's tenants until the health inspector shut them down. For once Celia hadn't a worry in the world. She'd never so much as cracked a lamp. Why should she?

Other stories in this collection will remind you of the time your neighbor helped you put Christmas lights on your roof, or the woman across the street who used to leave free zucchini on your stoop but hasn't appeared in months. People everywhere know their neighbors: the crotchety ones and the intriguing ones, the ones who do that thing with their hands. Hartwell Properties doesn't care to know its tenants: it would prefer that they never call to report  a fire or broken ice machine. Some owners are benevolent despots, walking past tenants' doorways to collect the rent while the children play inside. Others may only visit once a year, to check on a unit marked for demolition. In the summer, if I close all the windows except the one above the porch, I feel the breeze from passing cars. Sometimes I think I can smell perfume.

Hartwell Properties, like any large-scale landlord, knows that if it destroys one apartment today, the city will have to build another. The city plans to spend a hundred million dollars on affordable housing over the next five years, but until landlords like Hartwell can be held accountable, tenants will keep fleeing.  But as Mr. Boateng found out this summer, courts won't hear a case against a slumlord without the right complaint. And for even the best tenants, those are getting hard to find.

Celia's success was far from typical. Far from it. Hartwell appealed the verdict, which was overturned. The case went back to court on appeal and Celia lost again. The court threw out the ten billion dollar damage amount, ruling that the jurors had let passion outweigh reason. Celia got her legal fees, which would have been around ten thousand dollars.

Which would have been cheap enough had she been able to afford it. No lawyers will take a case unless they are sure they can justify it with the money they'll collect at the end. But payouts are capped by "punitive damage" limits that likely wouldn't have given Celia more than eighty thousand of Hartwell's assets, maybe two percent of their annual revenue. My sisters and I lay in our beds and did not speak. I heard the songs of the frogs and the intermittent sneeze of passing cars. We had eaten Miracle Soup, a staple of poor households since time immemorial: add water and an egg to leftover macaroni. No one's grandma could make it taste any worse than mine.

The radio clock in my bedroom said 7:49 a.m. Upstairs the toilet flushed, and I heard the bathwater tap squeak on. Then the water sloshing and Aunt Zata on the second floor groaning a little as she breathed. She would have to find the peppermint oil Penny had stolen and put it back. Aunt Zata would be searching the whole bathroom, the sink, the medicine cabinets, the shower curtain where Penny had sometimes hid things, running her hand over each surface. She would charge down the stairs, waving a towel and looking under the chairs, digging madly through the empty ashtrays. At 8:00 she would touch the bathroom doorknob and scatter to the kitchen, checking the flour canister and the berry-splattered tub of margarine, the cache of canned peaches in the pantry, the bowl where the mixer stood with its dough-hook attachment and black crumbs of bread.

Maybe, if she hurried, she would find the white plastic bottle before Grandma went into there at eight o'clock to wash her hands, her cup-saucer-and-teaspoon, glass, and plate from breakfast. Grandma would first pick up the paper napkin she'd left on my step to kneel on, stand on it to fill the kettle at the sink. She would open the soap dispenser and pump once, twice, three times. We are good at ignoring the lawyers for the plaintiff. They sound like ambulance chasers, nuisance jockeys, juries that find against their true clients. We're less good at remembering what plaintiffs' lawyers represent. They represent the same thing judges and juries represent, that the government represents: the people.

It wasn't always that way. A couple of hundred years ago, judges and attorneys argued cases by quoting the common law and canon law — unchanging sources that went all the way back to Europe. Any smalltown clodhopper could have looked up the law himself and seen what it was. But the rule of law changed as democracy changed; laws changed with the people, as votes do. Eventually the jargon changed with it, as all languages do. The people stopped understanding the law. So they needed help.

Plea Bargains

So plaintiffs' lawyers proliferated. Most of us have had to retain one. Mine was a solo who lived on the other side of the state, who chewed on a pencil through the whole interview, and then spent a week arguing down the lawyer for Jacobs Engineering, like a Mexican wrestling match — rifles like wings. He cost me eighty bucks and saved me thousands. Two months later, Jacobs sent a check... for eighty-seven dollars.

Lawyers are expensive for the same reason dresses are expensive and T-shirts are cheaper: They take longer to finish. You can sew a T-shirt in ten minutes. A dress is never done. They try the arms on, take some in, add some lace with a sewing machine, inspect it five times in a roomful of mirrors. Lawyers who make dresses take years. Lawyers who make T-shirts take minutes.

The work that the T-shirt lawyers do is called criminal law. Some criminals never see a court of law. Traffic tickets are the best example. After the first contour-pleating, you pay. After the second, they raise your rates and suspend your license. The third time you go to traffic school and listen to a policeman complain that they used to shoot people for less than this. You shut up and take your ticket because your lawyer is your stupid uncle who's been banned from the bars out here. After you go a few more times, they make you wear an ankle bracelet that shocks you if it hears someone opening your front door. The point of the article is made through the description of two lawyers attempting to resolve a class-action law suit on behalf of retired persons. (1) Two method ways to do law: obtaining unlimited visions of excellence gained through cooperation, coordination, categorization, and communication; or a business oriented, low-key, ad hoc, flexible, short-term, detailed and just efficient. Omni World, New York's newest immigrant enclave, defines the limits of hope and habit. It is neither the last stop on the journey to an assured future, nor the first station on the rails back downtown.

Boat problem

Almost every single one of the hundreds of apartment buildings in my city belongs to people who live somewhere else, who know nothing about living in our city or about the people they rent from, who have never heard or answered one of the many anguished phone calls from a tenant, day or night. In many cases, the owners don't even know who their lawyer is.

Something went wrong in the market for urban apartment rentals. Many rental problems--rats, broken toilets, holes in the wall--are the result of innocent neglect. But owners intentionally ignore other kinds of problems, so that many renters don't want to live in the apartments anymore. Owners of residential real estate have always had a financial incentive to extract the most rent from the property (and pay the least in costs, like taxes, maintenance, and insurance). If you can't get more from the tenant, then you increase the rent. If you can't get more from the rent, then you increase the rent.

There are duties attached to owning and renting a property. A certain amount of maintenance, a way of handling offers of rent, limits on rent increases. The market for urban apartment rentals is broken because it does not instantiate norms of renter behavior. There is no way to get the owner to pay for bad wiring, or to change an uncle's will to keep his niece in residence instead of selling the apartment.

The verdict came to $6.5 million, which would have been enough for Celia to get her boys a decent roof, to pay the creditors she still owed, to move into a house in the suburbs with plenty of land. But it meant nothing. Hartwell Properties, a Thompson-owned company, had filed for chapter 11 just before the trial. The company's bankruptcy made the whole verdict worthless.

Celia followed the news. Last February, Thompson's lawyers reported that the Chapter 11 had been "converted into a chapter 7 plan which involves liquidation of all assets of the debtor." Six months later, they posted a final notice on the case Web site announcing the trustee's exemption from all unsecured debts incurred during the bankruptcy. Anybody who thought the company had money coming was screwed.

Shareholder records and 10-Ks were filed in late June, showing that the company owes everybody $160 million, which is what Thompson told them last November. That's just company debt—Celia's not even included. In the cascading bankruptcy of his Dallas group, Thompson owes more than a quarter of a billion dollars. He tells car magazines that he can meet all his creditors and come out ahead. Celia believes that.

It would have been another year, she thought, before she could have saved that kind of money. But then her kids would have been nine, ten, and how would the fire inspector have explained that? Just one big fat accident. At least, knowing how they died, she might be able to teach them how to live.

When the headlight arrived at her apartment, Celia had already armored herself in good shoes (the new ones, Nikes) and a good coat (the old one, a long leather rain slick). She pulled on a hat that had tomorrow's weather in bird-and-snake diagrams, stood on tiptoe to look out the window (not far to fall) and decided to check the stairs first.

The first landing was empty, so she tapped the bell of the door on the second floor. No sound came from within, just a murmur of bass from the other end of the hallway. Celia shrugged and took a deep breath to hold off the nerves. She enjoyed going out at night, being alone, seeing ships come in.

The stairs were angled but safe, comfortable. The walk-in closet was directly above the fire escape door; Celia pulled pillows off her bed and laid them one on top of the other. She could see the street now.

The way the Mafia works is simple, which no one who grows up with them ever seems to realize. Zefirelli's first FBI agent explained it to Frank in a bar in Queens. "They take over your life, brick by brick," he said.

By then Frank had already done time for selling blow to the Gotti crew, and he didn't need a lecture. To hear Zefirelli tell it, the Mafia works like any other corporation, selling everything from a line in the site plan to the site plan itself. Labor unions buy electrical work, concrete's taken off the warehouse floor. Everyone pays.

The main difference is, the Mafia doesn't have sales meetings. A starter check, big enough that everyone knows there's more where it came from, changes hands. "You get an envelope in your locker. You open it up, look at the dirty money, nod your head." Makes people feel good. "Hey, this is no small operation," says Frank. Celia fainted right there in the courtroom. When she woke up, she held Mr. Boateng's hand.

She hasn't remortgaged her house yet, but that will change once the dockets are done and the checks have come. She still thinks about the flames, about her son who peeked around her and into the kitchen without even thinking. She does not want them to remember where they came from. She wants something better for them. She can now give them that. She was thirty-eight when she moved into the building, and she will be fifty-four when the last penny from the jury comes in.

When she built the new house, she saved the doorknob from her old one. She'll hang it somewhere in the new place. It is the only thing left. She can pick it out in her mind.

When I first met Celia, two years after the fire, she was overwhelmed by another case, and she gestured for me to take a seat on her kitchen stool. She was waiting to find out if she and seven other mothers had proof that she had been right about their sons' behavioral problems.

Six years earlier, she'd moved to Minnesota with her oldest son, Jon, and his girlfriend, Daisy. They signed a lease on a building managed by the locally owned Timber Pointe Properties. Celia's grandson Santi was seven months old and her boys Jon and Carlos, thirteen and fifteen, had started school. Celia went to work for Homestead Mattress—a soft sweatshop where half the staff was undocumented—and saved enough for a very used huntaway boat. Through tangerine sunsets and multicolored lily pads, she befriended her neighbors across the river at the Mall of America. Even before Santi turned one Celia knew that everything she loved was here.

After ten months, when Celia had spent every penny she had, Hartwell finally paid to move them next door to apartment 2A. On the second day there, Celia turned on the kitchen sink and nearly drowned the first thing she ever loved.

Two weeks later, bookless and loveless, the full-time mother of two gave up full-time mothering. She started as a receptionist at a hedge fund. She didn't explain--the wound was too raw--why she liked taking messages instead of making them. She dressed carefully and showed up to work ten minutes early. She added half and half to her coffee.

Her grandmother lived a block and a half away; she didn't answer the phone because she couldn't see the thing they called a caller ID. not liable. On the question of whether the units were provided with proper electrical maintenance under an injury and wrongful death statute, we the jury find the defendant not liable."  Some of the jurors looked away. Others nodded. They had made a decision.

The injuries and wrongful death statute was a state law, passed in like thousands of other special-interest laws that don't affect most people's lives. But Celia felt it affect her life in that courtroom. Negligence was a fuzzy standard. An injured party had to prove that the defendant knew or should have known that a building might burn down, and Celia could see how a reasonable person might not believe a space heater could cause that. 'You didn't turn your space heater off, did you?'

But Celia had paid money to the people that owned Hartwell Properties. She had given them her check to live in studio. They had money to send a lawyer.

"That is why the injuries and wrongful death statue is so important," a man said to her after the verdict. "Because it doesn't forgive foolishness. If you buy a space heater and leave it on, and it starts a fire... You did leave it on, didn't you? Because otherwise you'd only be hurt by it once, the first time you used it."

The man was twitchy, and the hair underneath his hat was gray. His eyes looked right through everybody he spoke to. He talked about Koresh and the Branch Davidians.

Demonstrating the difference between fighting an idea and fighting a wrong, he gestured at the corner of the room, where several uniformed people were taking photos of each other, posing with guns. Celia had been in there when the fire started and some of those guns. One was the friend that Celia heard the voice-taker talk about for a long time. She had forgotten.

The judge looked at the jury with a familiar mixture of awe and puzzlement and tried to conceal how clever he was by explaining why the case required a motion for a new trial.

The foreperson signed the verdict forms, and the jurors hurried to the elevators. No one was asking them if they wanted a ride. Celia collected her VCR and hair dryer and watched them leave.

The jury had been there three weeks, longer than anyone had expected, listening to their company's losses laid out one by one: a woman who ran a beauty salon, a man who owned a barbershop, a teenager working his way through college, a mother of nine who worked two jobs as a nurse's aide, four seniors who lived on Social Security and their only means of cooking was a microwave, a carpenter who repaired the neighbors' refrigerators, a group of artists. They crammed their stories and their debris and their grief into a jury room with cracked paint and a toilet that wouldn't flush and awarded their suffering a number. Whoever the jurors were - strangers, neighbors, mothers, mourners - they must have looked at the pile of receipts and the burn unit photos and the videos of weeping children and, whatever happened in that deliberation room, realized that they needed to send Hartwell's stockholders a message. $4,215,000 wasn't going to do what it had been intended to do. It wasn't going to restore what had been lost. But the jury wanted to tell someone who had been loved and lost and fucked over that they were seen and they were believed, and they had done the best they could.

Celia watched the jurors disappear into the lobby and kept thinking how strange it was that people would pick through the remnants of her life and then vanish back into their own. She couldn't reveal herself to strangers. She didn't trust anyone that much. Hartwell Properties appealed. In early December, Celia watched her family's lawyer give a reporter an interview and say he hoped the jury had sent the message to slumlords that they would be held responsible for putting people's lives in danger. Celia nodded. They had to be held responsible.

Hartwell Properties had a website: Safe Living brought to you by Hartwell Insurance,iatrics the choice for gentrifying neighborhoods. Find your dream home away from home today, said the banner heading.

Two months after the fire, an electrician rewired the apartments in 418 Hartwell Street. The junction boxes had scorched metal marks, and a trickle of melted insulation had run over the studs. By February, with help from the Red Cross, volunteers from five churches, and a little leftover money from the lawyer, Celia and her son Diego were able to buy appliances and put down new linoleum. At the end of May, as soon as it was warm enough to open all the windows, Celia and her sons moved back in.

Apartment 2B had no smoke or fire damage, but the smell of burnt plastic lingered beneath the new paint. Celia vacuumed the floors every day and left bowls of cloves and cinnamon on the counter. Diego was going through final exams and tried to study, but every night he packed his books and went to his girlfriend's until supper.

One Saturday night Celia was stirring a pot of stew when Diego burst into the kitchen. "Mom," he said, "someone just set fire to the trash cans again."

Celia took Diego outside and called the fire department, and they came and put out the flames. "They don't care about us," Diego said.

"They do," said Celia. "They keep sending fires our way because they want us to move."

"That's not fair," said Diego.

"It never is," said Celia, "but we will stay and fight this one, too."

She made a cup of tea and sat at the kitchen table while Diego sat at the counter with his books. On the porch roof, the neighbors played dominoes and watched, because the fire trucks would be coming any minute now.
